title: Normal distribution and z-scores
explanation:
Every normal distribution has the same bell shape; only its centre $\mu$ and spread $\sigma$ differ. To compare values on different bells, measure them in a common unit: **standard deviations from the mean**. That is the z-score, $z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, which tells you how many standard deviations $x$ lies above or below the mean [1].

Positive $z$ means above average and negative $z$ means below. For example, with mean 5 and standard deviation 2, the value 11 is three standard deviations above the mean [2].

Going backwards is just as useful: $x=\mu+z\,\sigma$ turns 'two SDs above average' into an actual value.
keyIdeas: $z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$: distance from the mean in SD units.
Sign of z: above (+) or below (−) the mean.

workedExample.problem: Adult heights in a group have mean $170$ cm and SD $10$ cm. Find the z-score of $155$ cm, and the height with $z=1.2$.
steps: Sense check: the negative z belongs to the shorter height.

pitfalls: Dividing by the variance instead of the standard deviation.
Subtracting in the wrong order ($\mu-x$), which flips the sign.
Treating z as a probability; it is a position on the scale.

citations.quote: how many standard deviations the value x is above (to the right of) or below (to the left of) the mean
For example, if the mean of a normal distribution is five and the standard deviation is two, the value 11 is three standard deviations above (or to the right of) the mean.
